To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the heritability of litter size increases with parity, that the genetic correlations of litter sizes between parities are high for adjacent parities but much lower for nonadjacent partries, that heritability of growth and backfat are similar, and that genetic correlation between growth and backfat is moderate, whereas the genetic correlation between growth or backfat and litter size is close to zero.

heritability estimates were low for NBA and increased with parity, whereas the heritability for growth and back-fat was high, with a low genetic correlation with litter size, and that the genetic correlation of litter size between parities decreased with increasing parity difference.

heritabilities of NBA increased with the order of parity, genetic correlations between NBA in different parities were generally high between adjacent parities, and low between nonadjacent ones, and genetic correlations between NBA and production traits (WT and BT in this study) were close to 0 in most cases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of genetic parameters for production and litter size traits.
the genetic correlation between litter size in different parities, which has been neglected by most researchers.
the estimation of genetic parameters for multiple traits and parities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
selection for growth and fatness would have a negligible effect on litter size in pigs.
the genetic correlations between production and reproduction traits are very low, but not zero.
genetic correlations between production and reproduction traits are low to moderate and that selection for production traits should result in no correlated response in litter sizes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the genetic correlation between production and reproduction traits in pigs is small, and therefore the genetic improvement of production traits will have no or very small effect on the reproductive performance.
genetic correlations between litter size traits in different parities are much lower than those between adjacent parities.
selection for growth and fatness should not have a significant correlated response on litter size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Bayesian methods can be successfully implemented for estimating genetic parameters of litter size in pigs.
genetic parameters estimated for litter size and growth traits in pigs are different from those reported in other species.
genetic parameters of litter size for different parities are different and should be estimated and considered in genetic evaluations.
